title: How Limousines Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how limousines work, starting with the broad definition of a limousine (any car with a roomier back seat plus a driver) and the origin of the word in the French town of Limousin, where a hooded cloak called a limousine gave the name to horse-drawn covered carriages. They trace the move to automobile limos in the 1920s, the shift from building limos from scratch to converting existing luxury cars by cutting them in half and adding length, and the conversion process (stripping the interior, rails, floor pan, driveline and brake extensions). They cover the 2013-era San Mateo Bridge limo fire caused by a modified floor pan, manufacturer certification programs (Cadillac Master Coach Builder, Ford Qualified Vehicle Modifier), length limits, interior excess, gas guzzler tax, driver licensing varying by state, and crash tests. The episode closes with presidential limousines from the Sunshine Special (Roosevelt) through the Truman Lincoln, Kennedy's Lincoln Continental, the Reagan/Ford Continental, the 1983 Cadillac Fleetwood in In the Line of Fire, the Bush-era Cadillac Deville, and the 2009 Cadillac. A listener mail from April about giving dog food to a homeless man with a dog closes the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and David Sedaris chatter
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about a comedian's family, Atlanta taxis and Uber, and their dislike of stretch limousines, before setting up the topic.

segments.title: Definition of a limousine and the word's origin
segments.summary: A limo is broadly any car with a roomier back seat plus a driver, such as a town car or car service. The word comes from Limousin, France, where a hooded cloak called a limousine was worn, and early covered horse carriages took the name.

segments.title: Early automobile limousines and luxury car targets
segments.summary: When cars replaced carriages, limo services appeared, early on in New York City in the 1920s. Early limos were built from scratch, but builders soon found it easier to stretch existing luxury cars such as Mercedes-Benz, Cadillac, Fleetwood and LeBaron. Bentley made about twenty Mulsanne-era limos.

segments.title: Limo conversion process
segments.summary: Converters, such as Armbruster (described as an early converter), cut an existing car in two and insert an extension. The process involves stripping the interior, mounting the car on rails, cutting it, extending the driveline, brake lines and wiring, and adding a new floor pan. Length is generally capped at about twice the original.

segments.title: San Mateo Bridge limo fire and manufacturer certification
segments.summary: A modified floor pan that rubbed against the drive train created heat and sparks that ignited the upholstery, killing a bride-to-be on the San Mateo Bridge; the CHP ruled it an accident. Because a converted car is legally a new manufacturer's vehicle, Cadillac and Ford run certification programs for converters, and the modified car must still meet federal motor vehicle safety standards.

segments.title: Limo interiors, licensing, crash tests and fuel costs
segments.summary: Limo interiors are heavily customized with TVs, hot tubs, bars and sound systems, including a pink Cadillac limo with a heart-shaped hot tub at Ripley's in Branson. Driver licensing varies widely by state. Limos go through crash tests and face gas guzzler tax and poor mileage; a 32-foot Hummer limo ran on alternative fuels.

segments.title: Presidential limousines
segments.summary: The hosts trace presidential cars from the armored Sunshine Special built for Franklin Roosevelt (1938 era, with hinged doors and bulletproof glass) through the Truman Lincoln Cosmopolitan with a bubble top, Kennedy's 1961 Lincoln Continental, which was later armored and kept in the fleet, and the Ford and Reagan Continental. Other cars covered include the 1983 Cadillac Fleetwood used in In the Line of Fire, the Bush-era Cadillac Deville, and a 2009 Cadillac. Retired cars are at the Henry Ford Museum.

segments.title: Extreme limos and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts mention Popular Mechanics coverage of extreme limos, including a Hummer, a DeLorean limo, a semi limo, and a Mexican conversion of a 727 jet. They suggest searching How Stuff Works for limo topics.

segments.title: Listener mail: April and the homeless man with a dog
segments.summary: A listener named April describes trying to give dog food and money to a homeless man with a husky, who said the dog was not his. The hosts close by inviting listeners to share stories and contact the show.
